title: Acyclicity of the naive cotangent complex of an ind-etale algebra
statement: Let $R\to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings which is ind-etale, that is, $S$ is a filtered colimit of finitely presented etale $R$-algebras [def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra]. Form the standard naive cotangent complex $\mathrm{NL}_{S/R}=[I/I^2\xrightarrow{\delta}\bigoplus_{s\in S}S\,\mathrm d[s]]$ of the canonical polynomial presentation $R[S]\to S$, with kernel $I$, as in [def-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map], in cohomological degrees $-1,0$. Then $\delta$ is an isomorphism of $S$-modules. Equivalently, $H^{-1}(\mathrm{NL}_{S/R})=H^0(\mathrm{NL}_{S/R})=0$, and $\mathrm{NL}_{S/R}\cong0$ in $D(\operatorname{Mod}(S))$ [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. No Noetherian, locality or finite-presentation hypothesis on $R\to S$ is imposed.

source.place: Tag 07BQ (lemma-colimits-NL), together with Tag 00U1 (definition-etale); their filtered-colimit acyclicity consequence used in more-algebra.tex lemma-henselization-NL, first paragraph.

proof.text: Choose a small filtered presentation $S=\operatorname{colim}_{j\in J}S_j$ by finitely presented etale $R$-algebras, using the definition of ind-etale. For each $j$ choose a finite polynomial presentation $P_j\twoheadrightarrow S_j$ with finitely generated kernel $A_j$, as supplied by finite presentation. The etale conormal criterion makes the differential $d_j:A_j/A_j^2\to\bigoplus_{k=1}^{n_j}S_j\,\mathrm dx_k$ bijective. Here the criterion applies because the induced affine morphism is etale and the chosen presentation has finite variable set and finitely generated kernel.

source.place: Tag 00U1 (definition-etale), acyclicity of an etale algebra; finite-presentation version via the conormal criterion. More on Algebra, lemma-henselization-NL, proof first paragraph.

proof.text: Identify the free differential terms with $S_j\otimes_{P_j}\Omega_{P_j/R}$ and $S_j\otimes_{R[S_j]}\Omega_{R[S_j]/R}$ by the polynomial differential basis theorem, including its formula for $\mathrm df$; thus their differentials are exactly the presentation differentials. Apply the presentation homotopy-equivalence statement, with unprimed presentation $P_j\to S_j$ and primed presentation $R[S_j]\to S_j$. Write $\delta_j$ for the canonical differential. Its identities give a contracting map $s_j=\varphi_1d_j^{-1}\psi_0+h'$ for the primed complex: substituting $d_j\psi_1=\psi_0\delta_j$ and $\delta_j\varphi_1=\varphi_0d_j$ gives $s_j\delta_j=\varphi_1\psi_1+h'\delta_j=1$ and $\delta_js_j=\varphi_0\psi_0+\delta_jh'=1$. Consequently every $\delta_j$ is an isomorphism. This uses arbitrary-variable presentation comparison; the canonical presentation need not be finite.

source.place: Tag 00S1 (lemma-NL-homotopy), comparison of the finite and canonical presentations; Tag 00RX (lemma-differentials-polynomial-ring), their free differential terms.

proof.text: Use the diagram and degreewise $R$-module colimit $K$ of the cotangent colimit-comparison statement. For every arrow $a:j\to k$, its chain map has components $u_a,v_a$ with $v_a\delta_j=\delta_ku_a$. Multiplying by the inverses gives $u_a\delta_j^{-1}=\delta_k^{-1}v_a$. Hence the inverses form a natural transformation between the degree-zero and degree-minus-one diagrams. The colimit universal property induces a map $s:K^0\to K^{-1}$; on every colimit coprojection the equations $sd_K=1$ and $d_Ks=1$ are the equations $\delta_j^{-1}\delta_j=1$ and $\delta_j\delta_j^{-1}=1$. Uniqueness in that universal property proves both equations. Therefore $d_K$ is invertible and $K\to0$ is a quasi-isomorphism. No tensoring with $S$ and no exactness or flatness assumption is used in this argument.

source.place: Tag 07BQ (lemma-colimits-NL), colimit of the canonical complexes; the colimit-of-invertible-differentials argument is the universal property applied to their compatible inverses.

proof.text: The cotangent colimit-comparison theorem gives a quasi-isomorphism $K\to\mathrm{NL}_{S/R}$ after restricting to $R$-modules. As $K$ has zero cohomology, the definition of quasi-isomorphism gives $\ker\delta=0$ and $\operatorname{coker}\delta=0$ on the underlying modules; outside degrees $-1,0$ all terms vanish. Thus $\delta$ is bijective. Its inverse is $S$-linear: if $\delta(x)=y$ then $\delta(ax)=ay$, so uniqueness of preimages gives $\delta^{-1}(ay)=a\delta^{-1}(y)$, and the same argument gives additivity. Finally the zero chain map $\mathrm{NL}_{S/R}\to0$ is a quasi-isomorphism of $S$-module complexes, hence is inverted by $Q$ in $D(\operatorname{Mod}(S))$. This proves all the stated equivalent conclusions.
